Programming Algorithms

Complexity, Search, Sort & Recursion

Big O Notation

Big O notation describes the worst-case performance of an algorithm as the input size (n) grows. It measures scalability.

Notation Name Speed Example
O(1) Constant Excellent Accessing an array index.
O(log n) Logarithmic Good Binary Search.
O(n) Linear Fair Linear Search (looping once).
O(n²) Quadratic Poor Bubble Sort (nested loops).
O(2ⁿ) Exponential Terrible Recursive Fibonacci (naive).

Time Complexity

How fast the algorithm is. We care about the number of steps.

Space Complexity

How much memory the algorithm needs.

Searching Algorithms

Linear Search O(n)

Checks every element one by one. Works on unsorted data.

def linear_search(arr, key):
    for i in range(len(arr)):
        if arr[i] == key:
            return i
    return -1

Binary Search O(log n)

Divide and conquer. Data must be sorted!

def binary_search(arr, key):
    lower = 0
    upper = len(arr) - 1
    
    while lower <= upper:
        mid = (lower + upper) // 2
        if arr[mid] == key:
            return mid
        elif arr[mid] < key:
            lower = mid + 1
        else:
            upper = mid - 1
    return -1
Exam Tip

Always check if the array is sorted. If it is, Binary Search is preferred for large datasets. If not, you must use Linear Search (or sort it first).

Sorting Algorithms

Bubble Sort O(n²)

Repeatedly swaps adjacent elements if they are wrong. "Bubbles" largest to the end.

def bubble_sort(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    for i in range(n):
        swapped = False
        # Last i elements are already sorted
        for j in range(0, n-i-1):
            if arr[j] > arr[j+1]:
                arr[j], arr[j+1] = arr[j+1], arr[j]
                swapped = True
        if not swapped:
            break

Selection Sort O(n²)

Finds the minimum element and moves it to the sorted part.

def selection_sort(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    for i in range(n):
        min_idx = i
        for j in range(i+1, n):
            if arr[j] < arr[min_idx]:
                min_idx = j
        # Swap found min with first
        arr[i], arr[min_idx] = arr[min_idx], arr[i]

Quick Sort O(n log n)

Divide and conquer using a pivot. Much faster for large datasets.

def quick_sort(arr):
    if len(arr) <= 1: return arr
    pivot = arr[len(arr) // 2]
    left = [x for x in arr if x < pivot]
    middle = [x for x in arr if x == pivot]
    right = [x for x in arr if x > pivot]
    return quick_sort(left) + middle + quick_sort(right)
Recursion (HL)

Recursion is when a function calls itself. It must have:

  • Base Case: Stops the recursion.
  • General Case: Calls itself continuously moving towards the base case.

Factorial (n!)

def factorial(n):
    if n == 1:
        return 1
    else:
        return n * factorial(n-1)

Fibonacci Sequence

def fib(n):
    if n <= 0: return 0
    elif n == 1: return 1
    else:
        return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)
Keyword Glossary
Keyword Definition
Time Complexity A measure of how many steps an algorithm takes to run based on input size.
Space Complexity A measure of how much standard memory an algorithm needs to run.
Linear Search Sequential search, checking every element (O(n)).
Binary Search Efficient search on stored data, halving the search space each time (O(log n)).
Bubble Sort Sorts by comparing adjacent items and swapping them (O(n²)).
Selection Sort Sorts by repeatedly finding the minimum element (O(n²)).
Recursion A function calling itself until a base case is met.
Base Case The condition that stops the recursion.
